Destin Daniel Cretton's MCU debut featured stunning action sequences, and Kwan could use this martial arts training, including his second-degree black belt in Taekwondo.

Clearly Ke Huy Quan enjoyed his time working with Destin Daniel Cretton, and would love to work together again within the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Following Spider-Man: Brand Newly introduced Day's record-breaking success, hopefully the filmmaker returns to Shang-Chi sooner rather than later. The Fable reboot had to look beyond Lionhead's RPG trilogy because games like The Witcher 3 "became the gold standard"

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (388 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their significant RPGs and set a newly introduced "gold standard.".
  • It has been revealed that the upcoming Fable reboot is finally ending its decade-long development journey soon.
  • Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their significant RPGs and set a newly introduced "gold standard.".

It has been revealed that the upcoming Fable reboot is finally ending its decade-long development journey soon. Playground Games had to set up an entirely fresh team to work on its fairytale revival, so Fable's production wasn't quite as smooth sailing as the studio's consistently excellent Forza Horizon series, for example.

Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.

"In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard," Fulton said. "And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG.".

"All of these games continue to reset player expectations," he continued. Millions of players suddenly had certain expectations about what their significant-budget, open-world role-playing games should look like. So, Playground couldn't pull inspiration from Fable and Fable alone.

"I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects," Fulton added.

Sources indicate that still, Playground's Fable is drawing most heavily from Lionhead's Fable. Fulton specifically mentions the game's signature British wit and in-flux morality system as examples. Then there's also the spontaneous life sim elements that "none of our competitors do," according to Fulton. "It's a totally Fable thing, the social simulation and economic simulation. Okay, there are games that have economic simulations, but they're not in [our] RPG category. Fable is unique in that it's almost like a life sim in terms of genre.".

Raising four separate families and becoming the entire map's benevolent landlord was one of the funnest parts of Fable back in the day, alongside those sometimes silly characters. Seeing next year's Fable lean into those systemic choices, and having Albion's NPCs react to them more believably, could give this one a very long shelf life.

Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and this 2026 model is on sale for $500 off for Black Friday, down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

According to recent reports, samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

Recent findings suggest that the system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That noted, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors, from New York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

One thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in Latest York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

Speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

In a recent development, we’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this concern: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian.

It has been revealed that van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

Recent findings suggest that so who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of New York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

Industry observers note that — As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

Recent findings suggest that the 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

— Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of my favorite video games is Control.
  • As reported by The Newly introduced York Times, last month the USFS published a few documents and reports related to Bigfoot as part of a Freedom of Information request.
  • First, a 1982 report written by someone who was sent out to study alleged Bigfoot tracks found in Mill Creek, Oregon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BigfootControlControl ResonantCreepy.

One of my favorite video games is Control. I also like this year’s Control Resonant, but not quite as much. And one of the best parts of those games is the government reports and files documenting creepy happenings and events in the game’s universe. Meanwhile, here in real life, the United States Forest Service has recently released some files about Bigfoot, and I was very pleased to see that feel like they fell right out of Control.

As reported by The Newly introduced York Times, last month the USFS published a few documents and reports related to Bigfoot as part of a Freedom of Information request. One file is just a clipping of a newspaper article from a Montana newspaper in the ’80s about massive, strange footprints found in the snow. The other two are far more interesting.

First, a 1982 report written by someone who was sent out to study alleged Bigfoot tracks found in Mill Creek, Oregon. Look at this and tell me it doesn’t look and read like something you’d pick up in Control.

Recent findings suggest that the report goes over, in a lot of detail, the footprints that were spotted. Ultimately, the report’s conclusion was that these tracks were fake, with the writer citing inconsistencies with gait pattern, signs of tampering with leaves, and other pieces of evidence that led them to conclude the tracks were “made by something other than a 300-pound plus two-footed being.”.

The other piece of Bigfoot documentation released by the USFS is what appears to be a short document written by someone who really thought Petty Creek, Montana was special and historically vital. One reason it was historically important: Bigfoot, baby. Here’s the bit about a Bigfoot sighting that allegedly happened in the ’40s.

Another type creature that walked on its hind legs, that altho there wasn’t actual sightings, tracks, a strong odor, and a grunting sound were observed. The first time was when four of us went in to pack out a six point bull elk on our backs and on arriving where the elk was supposed to be laying we found the intrails only and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks. At first we guessed it was a very large bear except bears don’t walk on their hind legs only for short distances and ordinarily would drag a carcass this large.

Industry observers note that this event took place in 1949 in the South fork of Petty cr. about where the present Garden point road goes. The following year when W.W. Schmitz was hunting in the upper Bills creek area he came across the same type of tracks and smelled a strong odor and heard a grunting type noise. He decided that he could find elk elsewhere and left the area. At this time we had never heard of Bigfoot so passed it off as something we didn’t want anything to do with and let it go at that.

The whole thing was typed up on a typewriter and even contains a bit of extra text at the bottom, written afterwards by hand. All of this, including the official seals, the black-and-white photos, and the matter-of-fact writing in the official report, feels like stuff I’d read in Control right before encountering Bigfoot. Sadly, it’s unlikely a big ape stalks the woods of the United States. But it’s fun to read about it, you know?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite the far higher prices of PlayStation and Xbox consoles today compared to their launch, or even the same period last year, both brands of console saw a significant boost in US sales leading up to the launch of this generation's biggest game: Grand Theft Auto 6.
  • In the week ending 14th November, PS5 hardware unit sales registered a 2.4x increase over the same week last year.
  • The PS5 Pro only accounted for less than 10 percent of the PlayStation's total unit sales, by the way, which Piscatella noted was "a LOT better than it has been in recent weeks", and seemingly the result of increased supply.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the far higher prices of PlayStation and Xbox consoles today compared to their launch, or even the same period last year, both brands of console saw a significant boost in US sales leading up to the launch of this generation's biggest game: Grand Theft Auto 6.

In the week ending 14th November, PS5 hardware unit sales registered a 2.4x increase over the same week last year. Xbox wasn't far behind, seeing a 2.3x increase in its own unit sales. That's according to industry analyst Mat Piscatella at Circana, who pulled the data from Circana's retail tracking service, which covers the US retail market.

The PS5 Pro only accounted for less than 10 percent of the PlayStation's total unit sales, by the way, which Piscatella noted was "a LOT better than it has been in recent weeks", and seemingly the result of increased supply.

GTA 6, of course, released on 19th November, so the surge in console hardware sales was clearly driven by the rush to attain consoles before the game came out. And while the GTA 6-driven demand isn't surprising, it's worth noting how much more expensive PS5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles are today.

According to recent reports, A standard PS5 today costs $650, compared to $550 a year ago. The PS5 Pro saw a big jump from $750 last November to $900 today. The base Xbox Series X jumped from $650 last year to $800 today, while Series S now costs $500, up from $400.

Even Switch 2, where GTA 6 is not available, saw a notable boost of 40 percent in hardware sales over the same period, driven by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and the special edition Zelda Switch 2 console.

Circana's November US video game market report, which releases in December, is already one of the most anticipated this year, for digesting and documenting the GTA 6 effect. Worldwide, GTA 6 sold more than 32.5m copies in one day, making Rockstar's parent manufacturer Take-Two $3.79bn (£2.89bn) in revenue. We haven't had any updated official sales figures since; but estimates suggest the sales figure could be well into the 40-millions. Perhaps Rockstar is waiting to hit the nice round 50m sales mark before announcing it.

If you're playing GTA 6, you may want to keep Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough to hand. It has plenty of very helpful guides covering the game's main missions, as well as explainers for mechanics like romance and the criminal profile, and even cheats for when you finish the game.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every few months, Grinding Gear Games resurfaces with livestreams to showcase all the new toys in the latest updates for Path of Exile 1 and 2. They play out quite differently from your usual game announcements, cutting straight to showing new gameplay features ahead of any preamble.

According to recent reports, according to Path of Exile co-game director Jonathan Rogers, this is a key part of Path of Exile's success over the last 13 years. Speaking at games industry conference DevGAMM FTW!, he explained how GGG came up with a winning formula for PoE's seasonal update schedule.

The announcement streams aren't just marketing, he explained, they help dictate what kinds of things the team should focus on with every enhancement. If it doesn't sound exciting enough to rally players around a newly introduced league, it doesn't get made.

After a teaser trailer reveals the theme and title of the league a few weeks before the full announcement, the stream dives right into the juiciest details—an approach that Rogers believes is paramount when it comes to selling the upgrade.

Rogers claims he's seen some "truly terrible livestreams for game announcements," before slipping in a quick jab: "Blizzard I'm looking at you.".

I've watched enough Diablo 4 fresh season streams to know exactly what he's talking about even if I don't quite agree that it's strictly a bad way to do it. Blizzard typically likes to lead with some introductions before having individual developers break down what's coming in an update.

According to recent reports, admittedly, these can drag on for too long, especially if you don't particularly care about percentage changes to some item or stat. But I appreciate hearing the thought process behind each decision from the people responsible for that aspect of the game. In a time when certain very vocal segments of the audience prefer to think of studios as machines, it's a good way to remind people that real human beings are behind it all.

Keep up to date with the most vital stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

That remarked, I think Rogers' specific point about too many studios wasting everyone's time by holding the best announcements for last is often true. For something like a upcoming enhancement to an ongoing game, everyone is watching to find out why this one is worth logging back in for. I want to see the standout details so I don't feel like I wasted 45 minutes for something I'm not that into.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes I do like the build-up and eventual payoff for a big reveal, though, like the way Blizzard dropped Diablo 5 at the end of the Diablo portion of this year's BlizzCon or how Larian surprised everyone with Divinity last year. Certain games earn the theatrics. If anything, Rogers' approach just underlines how important it is for studios to read the room and craft their announcements around the things that will actually spark interest rather than putting everyone to sleep.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Hunting Wives creator Rebecca Cutter is speaking out after season 2 hinted at a character’s potential history with emotional incest and sexual abuse.

During season 2, which premiered on Thursday, November 26, Brad (George Ferrier) hinted at trauma that he suffered as a result of his late mom Jill (Katie Lowes). He later experienced a dream sequence where he spoke with Jill about past inappropriate behavior — and his attempt to kill his mom in his head actually led to him accidentally murdering Chase (John Stamos).

According to recent reports, “I did want to leave it up to the audience,” Cutter exclusively told Us about the implication that Jill abused her son. “There’s clearly some sort of emotional incest situation with her. Whether she did or did not physically abuse him as a child, I don’t know.”.

Industry observers note that cutter wanted to highlight the idea that Brad was working through how his relationship with his mother affected his dating history, adding, “In his mind, he certainly feels a certain type of way about it because he conjured that dream sequence. I like to let things live in the audience’s mind and not answer. But it’s a very tragic story for Brad.”.

After attempting to work through the trauma, Brad hurt his father and tracked down Margo (Malin Åkerman), who ultimately killed him.

According to recent reports, “I wouldn’t say that we land entirely on the idea that Brad was a victim of sexual abuse,” Cutter clarified. “But I think the reason we wanted to dig deeper is because in season 1, he’s not really such a serious part of it and the truth is, he is actually the biggest victim of Margo from season 1 — his mother and his girlfriend have been murdered directly because of her.”.

She continued: “So we felt that it was only fair to see where that trauma takes him in season 2. This has real effects on people and the other people who are victims, we don’t get to hear from them anymore. Brad was a victim and he’s such a good actor that it was just like I really wanted to give him more — and I thought he delivered.”.

Lowes, 44, previously spoke to Us about adapting her character for the screen.

“I started reading the book and I quickly had to put it down when we started shooting. I was starting to get confused over the Jill that existed in the book and the Jill that Rebecca Cutter was putting on the show,” she exclusively shared with Us in August 2025. “I had to put the book down and just really focus on this story and the job that I was doing with this version of Jill.”.

Blizzard adjusts popular World of Warcraft: Forever Battleground to stop players power-grinding rewards

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many World of Warcraft: Forever players are at the moment in the midst of a substantial PvP reputation grind.
  • In a recent development, the battleground in question is Alterac Valley, a 40 person-a-side clash between Alliance and Horde factions, where both sides need to push their forces across a snowy, mountainous map into the opposing faction's base to take down the NPC General waiting there.
  • Industry observers note that played the intended way, Alterac Valley is a lengthy battle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many World of Warcraft: Forever players are at the moment in the midst of a substantial PvP reputation grind. However, this process has been disrupted due to a sudden change to one of the game's battleground PvP arenas.

In a recent development, the battleground in question is Alterac Valley, a 40 person-a-side clash between Alliance and Horde factions, where both sides need to push their forces across a snowy, mountainous map into the opposing faction's base to take down the NPC General waiting there. Alterac Valley is being grinded by max-level players for its gear rewards that are given once reaching "exalted" reputation there. Right now it's some of the best gear available ahead of raids being introduced next month.

Industry observers note that played the intended way, Alterac Valley is a lengthy battle. The Generals on both sides are fearsomely tough but by rushing to capture certain structures on the way to this battle, you can weaken the Generals enough to make them easier to overcome. As such, players have been fast-tracking this PvP instance, skipping smaller objectives and rushing core objectives to get to the Generals as fast as possible. This bypassed a lot of the incidental skirmishing allure of Alterac Valley, but it was an efficient way to promptly gain reputation and Honor points (PvP currency).

Sources indicate that but this strategy has been pretty much killed outright as of today. In a post made to the official World of Warcraft forums, community manager Kaivax revealed that the reputation gained from killing the Generals has been drastically reduced, while the reputation gained from killing other NPCs and capturing previously ignored objectives now grants more. Generals are also granted a buff that makes them incredibly strong for the first 20 minutes of a match, which is then reduced for each objective taken.

Recent findings suggest that this is a good change in regard to the experience of playing Alterac Valley. While rushing through was good for players looking to gain reputation promptly, they weren't really playing the Battleground in the way it's meant to be played. The dev post reads: "The overall intent for all of these changes was for games to feel more meaningful while trying to maintain a similar amount of rep gained over a similar playtime within the battleground, even with longer match lengths. There will be fluctuations depending on how successful you are at destroying towers and holding capture points at the end of a match however.".

Industry observers note that so how has the community reacted? Badly! Taking a gander at community hubs following this change demonstrates plenty of frustration. Take this comment by Reddit user Athrek: "I'm fine with the changes if they give it Rank Points and calendar events. But they've gutted the rep for both sides, extended the time it takes to play, and it still gives zero Rank Points. Now you may as well get to the win condition and then sit there for a few hours, gaining the passive rep cause there's nothing else of value to be had.".

It appears as of writing that the reputation gained isn't as much as it was previously, so those playing purely for reputation have been hit. There's another element of frustration which is that those who rushed to level 60 and ground Alterac Valley reputation and rewards before the changes won't be affected by this. Perhaps that's the allure of rushing to level 60!

Recent findings suggest that "This is why the WoW mantra is 'exploit early, exploit often'," writes user Lanienah12. "Some people are already exalted with AV rep and will receive no punishment for it; meanwhile latest people will be spending 3x as long." Especially in the wake of the Blackmaw Hold gold exploit being discovered by these frontrunners, there's a growing belief that those taking their time or that are limited by real-life factors are feeling the brunt of these changes.

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rockstar Games.

One thing that keeps striking me about Grand Theft Auto 6 is how good the writing is, even compared to that in previous games in the series. I enjoyed those earlier games, sure, but the dialogue and storytelling in GTA 6 are a cut above the rest in terms of both the game’s compelling characters and its worldbuilding. The fact that GTAÂ is set in an analogue of the real world helps the worldbuilding bridge gaps that most fictional universes couldnât, but Iâm increasingly finding that the standout writing is fighting a war within the game itself against some of the other jokes that have been building up in the series for over a quarter century.

Grand Theft Auto, for obvious reasons, canât use the existing brand names that we see every day in real life. In this sense it’s the opposite of the Like a Dragon series, which proudly wears all its licensed brand deals on its chest and even had to write a narrative around losing the license to a key landmark in the seventh game in the series. Talking Budweiser into lending their brand name to GTA 4 would have been an uphill battle and maybe also raised some uncomfortable questions about the gameâs proximity to real-world places and events. Better to just call your in-game equivalent Pisswasser and move on.

In a recent development, but weâre in 2026 now. The writing in theÂ GTA games has elevated and, to Rockstarâs credit, so have the fake brand names in general. Taco Bomb is a pretty good one as a stand-in for Taco Bell. ZIP for GAP is also good. Weazel News for Fox News makes sense on a couple of different levels, Snapmatic for Instagram is something that you recognize immediately upon hearing it. But there are a handful of brand names I think the series needs to ditch, as theyâre taking away from the more interesting narratives Rockstar wants to tell.

Pisswasser is not a bad joke on its own, but it wears its welcome out fast. Marbles, the McDonaldâs stand-in in GTA, sells a burger called Significant Balls. I get it, Big Mac, Big Balls, sure. But come on, man. Weâre scraping the bottom of the barrel here. Zombix isnât even a good pun. Itâs like someone filed that one in the ten minutes before the deadline. We need to start thinking intelligently about which of these benefit worldbuilding and which detract from it.

I’m not saying all of these need to go or even a majority of them. There are plenty of good joke brand names, but there are also ones that are very, very 2000s, and it would be better for the games if they disappear. Grand Theft Auto has grown with its audience, and it’s now delivering narratives that genuinely keep up with well-written modern movies, so why are we limiting aspects of it to jokes that would appear in an Epic Movie parody?

In a recent development, rockstar can and should start taking a look at these and see what makes sense for their games every so often. Audit the world, donât just assume that because it existed in previous games, it needs to exist forever.

Itâs not like brands donât just disappear from the real world all the time. Joannâs Fabrics isnât around anymore, but your world keeps spinning, just like it would if the Obey car line simply did not appear in a fresh game. You planning to take a Spirit Airlines flight this holiday? Youâre sure as hell not, nor would you be a sobbing mess on the floor if a Major Balls sandwich billboard wasnât overlooking a highway chase.

Industry observers note that there are already so many good jokes in these games that the lame ones can get cut out without losing anything. No one is wrong for liking them, but maybe the games themselves can be better for examining what works and what doesnât. No series has ever escaped a need for refreshing itself and iterating over the years and, in almost every way, GTA 6 nails it. Thereâs just one more thing I want to see them look at before they build their next GTA world, asking themselves if each jokey brand name still fits their vision. If it does, great! If they decide it would be better to snip, that would be fine, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I can still hardly believe a newly introduced Lord of the Rings movie is coming down the pipeline. Directed by Andy Serkis, the Aragorn road trip journey The Hunt for Gollum is already filming with the director also back in the mo-cap suit, and we got some first look set photos earlier this year. Now, as the movie continues to come together ahead of its 2027 movie release, franchise OG Orlando Bloom talks his own legacy in the franchise.

Orlando Bloom was a relative unknown when he was cast in The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring. He’d done some acting – fans in the UK might remember him from Midsomer Murders – but he was yet to be the Orlando Bloom of LOTR and Pirates of the Caribbean fame. It was the Peter Jackson movies that propelled him forth, and he told EW that when he looks on that time in the early aughts, it’s like a time capsule for the actor.

It has been revealed that it’s like a moment in time. For me, it’s like a capsule. It was a gift to go back and do something like The Hobbit.

We’d actually spoken to Bloom when he was recast as Legolas in The Hobbit trilogy and asked him how he felt about getting to return to the world a second time. He told CinemaBlend it was “sheer joy,” although there were some practical concerns about having aged a decade since the original LOTR films.

According to recent reports, it was sheer joy. It was also a little bit of, "Oh, my word." This is ten years later, I'm ten years older and how's this all going to work? I quite literally was like, 'Can I just try on my old costume just for posterity of it all?' It was amazing that Pete [Jackson] was back at the helm of this movie, and it was amazing that I got a call to say, 'We would love you to be a part of the film.'.

They did bridge that gap, and Bloom looked great in The Hobbit movies. I think it’s very interesting the upcoming movie The Hunt for Gollum will also be bringing another elf back a decade later once more with Lee Pace reprising Thranduil (Legolas' father), so while elves live on and on, the humans behind the movies face some practical challenges. Still, Bloom believes it's a privilege to be a part of Tolkien's story (and recent his words echo newcomer Anya Taylor-Joy's feelings as well.).

According to recent reports, I also just love that world. I think people, Tolkien’s world is so magical, it’s such an interesting and it’s kind of so relevant. It’s never not going to be relevant. It’s an unbelievable piece of literature.

According to recent reports, there's no indication right now Orlando Bloom will be back on set for another round, though he does have his own LOTR reunion coming in a different project. Regardless, given the timeline of the movie, which plays out just before The Fellowship of the Ring, the elven world will once again be a part of The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt For Gollum. The legacy that Orlando Bloom helped created should live on in this new movie, and I, for one, can't wait to see what that looks like.

The Lord of The Rings: The Hunt for Gollum hits theaters on December 17th, 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ubisoft is clearly serious about implementing generative-AI deeply into the game development process.
  • That's according to a latest Vertical Slice report, citing multiple anonymous sources presently working at Ubisoft.
  • Several employees stated that pitching a game idea without gen-AI or without explaining why it does not involve the use of the controversial tech will not receive the greenlight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ubisoft is clearly serious about implementing generative-AI deeply into the game development process. The French publisher now expects teams pitching new project ideas to be prepared to explain how gen-AI will help with developing the game.Teams who don't want to use gen-AI will need to clearly justify their reasoning to the higher-ups.

That's according to a latest Vertical Slice report, citing multiple anonymous sources presently working at Ubisoft.

Several employees stated that pitching a game idea without gen-AI or without explaining why it does not involve the use of the controversial tech will not receive the greenlight. This is especially relevant for smaller games with tight teams who now reportedly must deal with Ubisoft leaders' desire to implement gen-AI if they want to get their pitches reviewed.

"We were told that using AI will increase the speed at which pitches can be made by 'small lean agile teams,'" one source said. "We were told that as the goal was to move fast, iterate and discard projects to sift out the good stuff. AI was essential in maintaining a rapid pace.".

While some noted Ubisoft is not openly mandating gen-AI use to staff, others feel "cornered" by gen-AI. One source said Ubisoft views the tech as "unavoidable", and that only a minority of the company's audience reject it.

According to recent reports, ubisoft recently gave name to an internal initiative to expand the use of generative-AI and research how its developers can make use of the technology. It's called Motherbrain, and it has its own division within Ubisoft.

Over a year ago, Ubisoft embarked on a major restructuring effort that has seen the formation of new subsidiaries, the consolidation of its biggest brands into 'creative houses', the closure of studios and, of course, multiple rounds of layoffs.

Industry observers note that "Ubisoft is in a top-down nightmare of AI psychosis," one source added, pointing to the already low morale within the tech giant. "Yves [Guillemot] has hitched his wagon to the tech, demanding the rest of the company follow on.".

Deborah Nevins—a Legend of Landscape Architecture—Plants With Purpose

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Newly introduced York where we could imagine our future children growing up.
  • It looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale.
  • Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Newly introduced York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

Nevins in her garden in East Hampton.

It looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

Our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

In a recent development, but what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”.

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

“Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”.

It has been revealed that this is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

Recent findings suggest that GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

Recent findings suggest that to Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she says. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”.

Industry observers note that over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she says. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”.

Sources indicate that “There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” says Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and Latest York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”.

He recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell claims. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”.

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

According to recent reports, gil Schafer, a Latest York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he indicates, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”.

Industry observers note that nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

Fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins says, offering me an concern of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this substantial apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”.

When Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to Newly introduced Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she claims. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

One of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he says, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”.

At the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a newly introduced one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of significant moves,” she states. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”.

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

Hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger notes. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”.

Recent findings suggest that nevins’s office is based in New York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she notes. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”.

PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer says of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

Industry observers note that on average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build upcoming structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning states of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

Sources indicate that patience is a major part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer claims. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

According to recent reports, people joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”.

Recent findings suggest that “I do love them,” Nevins notes of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I stated, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”.

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

According to recent reports, currently her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”.

Sources indicate that nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she notes. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”.

In another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The Fresh York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we remarked to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he indicates. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”.

According to recent reports, in the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby mentioned that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”.

THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”.

The Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

According to recent reports, “Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler indicates. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”.

#154764. Fed up of Steam's lack of action regarding AI slop? Maybe you should take a look at the 'Games Without AI' event, instead

Fed up of Steam's lack of action regarding AI slop? Maybe you should take a look at the 'Games Without AI' event, instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that yesterday, a new Steam event went live that claims all games featured in it have avoided AI entirely during development.
  • In a recent development, "Behind every game, there are people, ideas, passion, and countless hours of creative work," said a mission statement.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of games featured in the event, and not just ones tied to the organisers, as the cynical-minded amongst you may expect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that yesterday, a new Steam event went live that claims all games featured in it have avoided AI entirely during development. The event, called 'Games Without AI', has been set up by a third party rather than Valve - by Dev Land Marketing, All Ages Of Geek, and Dark Cocooning - to "support real creators" and runs from 25th November to 6th December.

In a recent development, "Behind every game, there are people, ideas, passion, and countless hours of creative work," said a mission statement. "We've carefully curated a selection of independent games that celebrate human creativity, craftsmanship, and collaboration, all made without generative AI. But Games Without AI is more than a festival. It's also about bringing developers, players, and creators together to build a community where we share knowledge, support one another, and grow together.".

Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of games featured in the event, and not just ones tied to the organisers, as the cynical-minded amongst you may expect. Ones that jump out to my eye are: Pidgeon Pocket, a 'cozy incremental' with pixel art and a flock of adorable pigeons that you need to upgrade; Bottled by Bears, which tasks you with collecting and discovering rare bees, bottling honey jars, and expanding your farm; and Arctic Awakening, which sort-of looks like Pacific Drive meets Subnautica, in the Arctic.

According to recent reports, the event was posted to Reddit where commenters immidiately began accusing certain games of having used AI in their development - often without proof. One user, however, who claims to have been a developer trying to submit a game for inclusion in the event, offered some insight on how the selection process worked.

"As one of participants I can assure you that the qualification process was restrictive[ly] hard to bypass," they wrote. "We were all required to provide proofs of the game being made without AI and share as much of the process as possible. Then it was actually voted by community, which games are convicing enough so the whole process was intended to be as objective as possible. It's an event meant for developers who take pride in their games being made by humans so if any participant attends with ill intend of showing that AI generated game can get through... That would be very sad and shameful. From what I've seen, none of the selected games can be reasonable suspected of that. I also know some other participants personally and they are genuine zero-AI devs.".

Sources indicate that it's refreshing to see curation turned towards explicitly anti-AI games: between major publishers chasing the trend and smaller indie studios being caught out using the dubious tech, it's nice to see a library of games that promises that no AI was used during development. Given that Valve itself recently claimed it was up to developers themselves to ensure their games couldn't be ripped off by cheap AI tools, I'm happy to see an initiative rallying against the normalcy of all this.

In a recent development, the most recent Steam Next Fest had more than double the number of demos than last year, but that stat isn't what it seems on the surface: roughly 17 percent of those games listed the use of generative AI, but it seemed that many more games did not disclose the use of AI in their development. In June's event, more than a thousand games in Steam Next Fest featured a generative AI disclosure of some kind, which made up roughly 20 percent of all featured games.

Over the past 18 months or so, we've seen the glitch of generative AI in games on Steam evolve quite a lot. AI tools have been used to clone games, resulting in a troubling trend of imitation games taking the spotlight away from real indie devs. Whilst Steam, as a storefront, has been steadfast in requiring games to declare their use of generative AI during development, there are loopholes: devs that claim they only use AI tools for "efficiency gains" can appear on the store without any declaration.

At the other end of the spectrum is Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, who last year criticised Valve's requirement to disclose generative AI, saying, "Steam and all digital marketplaces need to drop the 'Made with AI' label. It doesn't matter any more." The swell of owners rejecting AI in games, though, seems to run counter to that argument. Recently, Big Walk developer House House revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" during the development of the co-op darling, and received a lot of backlash online.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Right now, only a select number of sanctioned mods can be used in Vermintide 2's "official realm" which is the one with loot and leveling that carries over, while unsanctioned mods can only be accessed in a "modded realm" where there are no progression systems.
  • "We have an update releasing in early December which will see the Modded Realm have its own, local, offline progression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that though Vermintide 2's had a Steam Workshop since 2018, it's mostly used for quality-of-life stuff like UI tweaks. That's set to change now that Fatshark has announced a public release of its internal developer tools, which they say "will allow modders to work their magic on both editing and creating anything from custom levels, models, textures, particles, animations, and more!".

Right now, only a select number of sanctioned mods can be used in Vermintide 2's "official realm" which is the one with loot and leveling that carries over, while unsanctioned mods can only be accessed in a "modded realm" where there are no progression systems. Obviously that's off-putting to a lot of players, so Fatshark has announced a change.

"We have an update releasing in early December which will see the Modded Realm have its own, local, offline progression. That means that playing in the Modded Realm will still result in you gaining loot and experience, but noted progression will not reflect on the Official Realm. This should make playing on the Modded Realm feel much better and not be discouraging for those that want to try out all of the unsanctioned mods, both the ones that already exist and the ones to come thanks to the Mod Tools!".

According to recent reports, I'm not sure how many players will be happy to start over from level one just to get access to a wider variety of mods, but I hope it encourages some folks to check them out. Another thing that'll encourage newly introduced players is that XP has been doubled from now through till Monday, and Vermintide 2 is on sale for 90% off on Steam. The DLC has been discounted too.

In less good news, the servers for Versus Mode are being turned off. "We have monitored the use of the dedicated Versus servers lately," Fatshark said, "and come to the conclusion that they are barely used. We have therefore decided to shut these down." Versus Mode will still be playable, but via the menu option for a custom game or the lobby browser. You'll have to find a crew to play with on Discord first, which is how everyone seems to play Versus at the moment anyway.

That shutdown is planned for early December, at the same time as the upgrade that adds local progression to the modded realm. That update will also include balance changes to buff some unpopular talents, latest weapon icons, and a Tome of Triumphs in the hub area that will point you at any event if there's a live one, or to the weekly event mode if there isn't. The next event planned is the annual return of Gifts of the Wolf Father in December.

It has been revealed that finally, Fatshark mentioned that focusing on the mod tools to get them ready for public release had to take priority from other updates. "The weapon pack and the level that we mentioned in the past has been put on hold," they wrote. "We still want to get back to that, especially the weapon pack, but for now there is no active development on that. It’s crucial for us that we have transparency here, and while we are not working on these things, we do stick with our games! We have looks both near and far for Vermintide 2.".

Tech Report: From a gown purchased with wartime rations to a secret engraving on the ring: Inside the historic royal wedding of Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple.
  • November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.
  • It has been revealed that the Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip married in 1947, going on to make history by achieving the longest marriage of any British sovereign couple. Back then they were, of course, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, tying the knot in the rather austere years of post-war Britain. So, what really happened on their wedding day?

November 2, 1947: Queen Elizabeth—then Princess Elizabeth—with Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, King George VI and Queen Elizabeth (right) and members of the immediate and extended Royal Family at Buckingham Palace after their wedding.

It has been revealed that the Queen and Prince Philip’s love story began back in 1939. Princess Elizabeth was just 13 years old; her dashing distant cousin, Prince Philip of Greece and Denmark, was five years her senior and about to join the Royal Navy. They met as she toured the Royal Naval College at Dartmouth; he was the young officer assigned to escort her around that day.

Determined to marry for love, Elizabeth was stated to be rather taken with Philip, who was described at the time as ‘handsome as any film star.’ The pair were soon writing letters to each other, and later, occasional chaperoned meetings took place.

The couple on their engagement, 1947.

Recent findings suggest that in 1946 Philip proposed in Scotland, and she immediately said yes. However, her father, King George, reportedly insisted the couple resist announcing their engagement until the Princess, who was just 20, was a little older. In the end, her parents gave in to her wishes, and Philip officially proposed to Princess Elizabeth in 1947, with a three-carat diamond ring he designed using stones taken from a family tiara that belonged to his mother, Princess Alice of Battenberg. It was created by London jeweller Philip Antrobus Ltd.

Princess Elizabeth with Philip Mountbatten on their wedding day.

The Royal Family were adamant that the wedding of Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip would reflect the country’s post-war situation while also offering a chance for the nation to celebrate.

Like many brides at the time, Princess Elizabeth had to save her rationing coupons to buy the materials for her dress but was given an extra 200 from the government to help. While well-wishers generously sent their own to the royal, they had to be sent back as rules dictated that coupons could not be shared outside of households.

It has been revealed that designed by Norman Hartnell, Princess Elizabeth’s wedding dress was made from ivory silk, duchesse satin and silver thread; the dress featured crystals, 10,000 seed pearls, a fitted bodice, heart-shaped neckline, long sleeves and a 15-foot train. It was made in just seven weeks by 350 skilled women since the wedding took place only four months after the couple’s engagement announcement. Norman Hartnell also designed Elizabeth’s going-away outfit.

It has been revealed that princess Elizabeth’s wedding day tiara was called the Queen Mary Fringe Tiara. It had belonged to her grandmother, Queen Mary, and had been given to her as a wedding present in 1893. It was remade from a tiara/necklace that Queen Victoria had bought from Collingwood and Co.

According to recent reports, as Elizabeth was getting ready on the morning of the wedding, it snapped. Luckily, royal jeweler Garrard was apparently on hand to fix it, and the Queen later revealed, “I think he taped up the spring.”.

Princess Elizabeth’s other wedding day jewelry included two pearl necklaces. The shorter of the two necklaces was the “Queen Anne” necklace, said to have belonged to Anne, the last Stuart Queen. The other was known as the “Queen Caroline,” and is said to have belonged to the wife of King George II. Both necklaces were left to the Crown by Queen Victoria and were given to Elizabeth as a wedding present by her father.

All royal bridal bouquets contain myrtle from a myrtle bush planted by Queen Victoria at Osborne House. Princess Elizabeth’s also had white orchids and was laid on the grave of the Unknown Warrior at Westminster Abbey the day after the wedding.

There were eight bridesmaids at Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip’s wedding: Princess Margaret, Princess Alexandra, Lady Pamela Mountbatten, Diana Bowes-Lyon, Lady Elizabeth Lambart, Margaret Elphinstone, Lady Caroline Montagu-Douglas-Scott, and Lady Mary Cambridge.

Her two pages were Prince William of Gloucester and Prince Michael of Kent, both aged five at the time.

The bridesmaids were given silver Art Deco-style compacts with the couple's initials and a crown engraved on the lid, set with five cabochon sapphires.

The Duke of Edinburgh's best man was David Mountbatten, the Marquess of Milford Haven.

Knowing that Elizabeth hated cigarettes, Prince Philip reportedly gave up smoking on the morning of his wedding “suddenly and apparently without difficulty,” according to his valet, John Dean.

The wedding took place at Westminster Abbey on November, 20th, 1947 at 11:30 a.m. Princess Elizabeth was the 10th member of the Royal Family to be married at Westminster Abbey.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip walking down the aisle of Westminster Abbey, followed by their bridesmaids and pages.

There were 2,000 guests in attendance, including the likes of the King of Iraq, Princess Juliana and Prince Bernhard of the Netherlands and the Hereditary Grand Duke of Luxembourg and Princess Elisabeth of Luxembourg. The ceremony was broadcast on the radio to millions of listeners.

Recent findings suggest that together with her father, Princess Elizabeth left Buckingham Palace in the Irish State Coach. (In her later years, it had been Queen Victoria’s state carriage of choice, as she declined to use the Gold State Coach following the death of Prince Albert.).

The wedding ceremony was officiated by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Geoffrey Fisher, and the Archbishop of York, Cyril Garbett.

The organist and Master of the Choristers at the Abbey, Australian William Neil McKie, was the director of music for the wedding and there were 91 singers; the abbey choir was joined by the choirs of the Chapel Royal and St George's Chapel in Windsor.

The service started with a specially composed fanfare by Arnold Bax and finished with Felix Mendelssohn's “Wedding March,” with ceremony hymns including “Praise, my Soul, the King of Heaven” and “The Lord's my Shepherd.”.

The bride and groom knelt on orange boxes covered in pink silk at the altar as a nod to post-war austerity.

Sources indicate that on the day of the wedding, Philip was given the title of Duke of Edinburgh by his father-in-law, King George VI. After the Queen ascended the throne in 1953, she made the decision in 1957 to make Philip a prince of the UK, in addition to his dukedom.

The wedding rings were made from a nugget of Welsh gold which came from the Clogau St David's mine, near Dolgellau.

According to Royal biographer Ingrid Seward, who wrote Prince Philip: Revealed, Philip had a secret message inscribed inside his wife's wedding band, a message that only the engraver, Queen Elizabeth, and her husband knew the contents of.

After the service, a wedding breakfast was held in the Ball-Supper Room at Buckingham Palace for 150 guests only, with Filet de Sole Mountbatten, Perdreau en Casserole and Bombe Glacée Princess Elizabeth on the menu.

During the breakfast, the string band of the Grenadier Guards played music while guests were greeted with individual posies of myrtle and white Balmoral on their place settings as the wedding favors.

The couple waving from the balcony of Buckingham Palace.

Famously, the newlyweds went onto the balcony at Buckingham Palace to wave to the huge crowds on the Mall.

In a recent development, although the royal couple received 11 wedding cakes, the official traditional fruit cake was baked by McVitie and Price and was four tiers and nine feet high. The wedding cake was decorated with both coats of arms, including the monograms of the bride and groom, sugar-iced figures of their favorite activities, and regimental and naval badges.

Mr Schur, chief confectioner at McVitie and Price, putting the final touches to the wedding cake.

The newlyweds cut the cake using the Duke's Mountbatten sword, which was a wedding present from the King.

Industry observers note that over 10,000 people sent telegrams congratulating Elizabeth and Philip, and around 2,500 wedding presents were sent from around the world. These included a cloth from Mahatma Gandhi that he’d woven himself, which Queen Mary mistook for an “indelicate” loincloth.

After their wedding breakfast, Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip headed to Waterloo station, joined by Elizabeth’s corgi, Susan, catching a train to Hampshire to spend their wedding night in Broadlands, the home of Philip's uncle, Earl Mountbatten.

The rest of their royal honeymoon was spent at Birkhall on the Balmoral Estate in Scotland.

Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip being showered with rose petals as they leave Buckingham Palace, London, for their honeymoon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple TV, in my opinion, consistently puts out some of the highest-quality shows of any streamer, and it seems like too many people sleep on a couple of the best: Slow Horses and Bad Monkey. The latter of whichis just about to kick off its second season on December 2 on the 2026 TV schedule, and that makes now the perfect time to jump on a great Black Friday deal for an Apple subscription.

Recent findings suggest that unless you’ve been living under a rock lately, you have probably seen a ton about GTA: VI and how it's set in a fictional version of Florida, and it’s filled with wild characters and kooky situations that only Florida can provide. You don’t have to be a gamer to get a similar experience with Bad Monkey. The show stars Vince Vaughn as a washed-up detective who gets himself wrapped up in some truly oddball cases in Florida.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also a book-to-screen adaptation based on a work by Carl Hiaasen, who is the king of bringing the weirdest bits of Florida to life, especially the kinds of totally goofy characters that make that state so unique, fun, and strange. Hiaasen was creating “Florida Mans” long before that became a thing. The show is just as fun as any of Hiaasen's books and really captures the spirit of everything he writes about.

The second show I feel like too many people sleep on is Slow Horses, based on the Slough House series by author Mick Herron. This isn’t a comedy like Bad Monkey, though Gary Oldman plays easily one of the funniest characters on TV these days. It’s a spy show about a group of disgraced MI5 agents in London led by a washed-up old Cold Warrior named Jackson Lamb (Oldman).

According to recent reports, the show just wrapped Season 6, but it’s already filmed its 7th, is presently filming its 8th, and has been renewed for seasons 9 and 10. Not only do we know we’re getting lots more of the show, but they have also banged out each season like clockwork, so we won't be waiting years for the next one. We’ll almost certainly be getting the next season next fall, just like the previous six. Jack Lowden, who was a favorite to become James Bond before Robert Pattinson got the gig, also stars on the show, so if you want to see him as a British agent, here’s your chance!

Of course, people love Ted Lasso and Severance, as do I, and those are also available, but for now, for me, my two favs are Bad Monkey and Slow Horses.
